guides.title: Everyday writing: receipts, complaints and ordinary lives
guides.description: Explore 87 paired originals and translations: food, animals, wages, deliveries, debts, quarrels and invitations across the ancient world and colonial Americas.
guides.intro: A missing tunic, a donkey sale, a demand for beer, a silk payroll. Written objects preserve practical concerns alongside monuments and royal histories. This collection places the original witness beside its English translation so that a small transaction can become a person’s story.
guides.scope: Ancient writing and separately dated colonial Indigenous American texts are brought together here. These are selected witnesses, not a ranking of the earliest languages or a claim that the same kinds of archives survive everywhere. The ordinary examples are searchable below; royal and ceremonial texts provide explicitly labeled comparisons.

map.scope: Selected places represented in the collection, spanning Mediterranean papyri, Mesopotamian tablets, Chinese documents and Indigenous American writing. Points retain each example’s findspot or collection context. They do not draw a transmission route between scripts; unlocated witnesses remain unplotted.

points.label: Girsu (Tello)
points.description: A barley allocation for women and children. The barley account sets out different allocations for groups attached to an institution. The tablet records their rations from the perspective of the people who managed the grain.

points.label: Probably Umma (Tell Jokha)
points.description: Barley wages for irrigation work. The record calculates how many working days it takes to clear grass and thornbush. It names a foreman, records the wage and bears a scribe’s seal. The sila was a measure of capacity.

points.label: Probably Kaneš (Kültepe)
points.description: Don’t give the donkey drivers money. The merchant Puzur-Ashur orders his brothers to withhold money from his donkey drivers. The same letter concerns a family business dispute and travel companions reportedly detained on their way to Kaneš.

points.label: Probably Dilbat
points.description: Repaying a loan in barley at harvest. Two men received a loan of barley from a woman named Dan-erissa. The line quoted comes from the clause stipulating repayment on harvest day. Cylinder seals left impressions on the clay.

points.label: Nineveh (findspot)
points.description: Timber counted after a fire. The writer distinguishes beams by size and separates intact timber from the pieces damaged by fire.

points.label: Deir el-Bahri, western Thebes, Egypt
points.description: A father defends the household rations. A priest who managed agricultural income writes to his relatives after a poor Nile flood. The letter sets out reduced rations and how the grain is to be distributed.

points.label: Valley of the Queens, western Thebes, Egypt
points.description: Do not give one to Sihathor. The overseer of the treasury sends distribution instructions, probably concerning preparations for a burial. Damage to the surrounding lines leaves the precise item uncertain.

points.label: Tell el-Amarna, Egypt
points.description: Two horses sent to Egypt. Aššur-uballiṭ of Assyria sends an envoy and gifts to open relations with the Egyptian court. The letter was found in Egypt and records Akkadian.

points.label: Deir el-Medina, western Thebes, Egypt
points.date: Twelfth century BCE, year 29 of Ramesses III
points.description: Tomb workers leave their posts. The royal tomb crew stops work when food rations fall overdue. The scribe Amunnakht records the workers’ demand and the series of protests that followed.

points.label: Wadi Hammamat, Egypt (area depicted on the map)
points.date: Twelfth century BCE, reign of Ramesses IV
points.description: The houses of the goldworkers. A work map places goldworkers’ housing near routes, rock formations and a temple. The papyrus’s connection to Deir el-Medina is likely. The map marker represents the area depicted in the ancient drawing.

points.label: Oxyrhynchos, Egypt
points.description: Paying donkeys and drivers to move hay. Animals, drivers and laborers appear together in an itemized cost calculation.

points.label: Tebtynis (Arsinoites), Egypt
points.description: Four drachmas for rent. A small payment survives as a terse record rather than a personal narrative.

points.label: Northern Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico
points.description: A cup for fresh cacao. The next part of the label identifies the owner as a sajal, a member of the local nobility. The diagonal writing comes upright as the cup is tilted. The map points to the Oxkintok area, which the museum proposes as the likely region of this ceramic style.

points.label: Mirador Basin, Petén, Guatemala
points.description: A chocolate cup with its owner named. The rim dedicates the cup, gives the kind of chocolate it was meant to hold, and names its owner as Muwaan K’uk’. Below, a woman pours chocolate from one vessel to another to make it froth. The map shows the approximate Nakbé region where the museum places production.

points.label: Santa Catalina Texupan, Mixteca Alta, Oaxaca, Mexico
points.description: Forty-two pesos for work on silk. The community account places a painting of silk workers and signs for the amount alongside the Nahuatl entry and a total of 42 pesos. The map points to today’s Santiago Tejupan, near the historic community.

points.label: Santiago Xochac and the Coyoacán region, Mexico
points.description: Ten pesos and four reales for a plot. Pedro de Santiago and Toribio Silvestre confirm receiving money for their land near the Xochimilco boundary. They say the proceeds paid for two high masses for their father. The marker is at Coyoacán, the regional reference point for the sale.

points.label: Apçolco, Coyoacán, Mexico
points.description: Four pesos for the butcher’s land. In the document recording his sale of house and land to the Dominican vicar, Juan Alvaro lists who sold him the separate plots and the prices he paid. The marker is at Coyoacán, the wider town named in the record.

points.label: Liye, ancient Qianling, Hunan, China
points.date: Qin period, late third century BCE
points.description: The brushes and ink you asked for. Xin writes to Lü Bo, acknowledges an earlier letter and sends the requested writing supplies with a courier named Shao.

points.label: Shuihudi cemetery, Yunmeng County, Hubei, China (approximate locality)
points.date: Qin period, late third century BCE
points.description: Send cash and leave the summer clothes. While away from home, Heifu gets word to his family about what he needs. This line preserves the preference in plain terms. The letter’s carrier has not been established.

points.label: Xuanquan Posthouse, Dunhuang, Gansu, China
points.description: A traveler brings several messages. Jian learns that Zhonggong is well through written messages carried by a traveler. The find comes from the Han postal station in the Dunhuang region.

points.label: Mogao Cave 17, near Dunhuang, Gansu, China
points.description: Late for the feast, owe a beaker of wine. A local association asks its members to assemble near Jiejia Hermitage for an annual meeting and feast. The circular was passed among members, and a person who skipped the event entirely owed a larger fine.

points.label: Walbrook, Roman Londinium, London, England
points.description: A debt of 105 denarii. Tibullus acknowledges a debt to Gratus for merchandise already sold and delivered. Both men were freedmen. The tablet preserves its date and the amount owed.

paragraphs.text: Some originals are photographs of the surviving object. Others are published original-language transcriptions in modern type. A normalized sign view is an editorial reading, not a facsimile of the ancient hand. Notes identify those differences, damaged passages and editorial uncertainty. English excerpts are labeled as excerpts, with translator and edition beside them.

The collection preserves its dated local contexts. A colonial Nahuatl or Quechua document cannot serve as a direct window into an unchanged pre-contact society. A vessel label, an account, a letter and a legal narrative also record different kinds of action. Read the object description before treating a colorful line as evidence of a general custom.

sections.heading: 3. Archival Coverage, Monsoon / Seasonal Constraints & Limits of Sea-Lane Maps

paragraphs.text: Historical route lines connecting Girsu (Tello), Probably Umma (Tell Jokha), Probably Kaneš (Kültepe) aggregate recurring seasonal sailing tracks, diplomatic dispatches, and coastal provisioning harbors documented in Everyday writing: receipts, complaints and ordinary lives rather than claiming every vessel followed identical GPS coordinates in every year.

Unequal archival survival—where European admiralty logs or monumental stone harbors outnumber wooden dhow, outrigger, and domestic reed-papyrus records—makes comparative archaeological shipwrecks and bilingual inscriptions essential for reading ocean history evenly.
